decision.reason: The paper conducts a preregistered conceptual replication retesting whether the changing-state irrelevant sound effect on visual-verbal serial recall is independent of distractor intensity (45 vs. 75 dB(A), N = 130) and directly compares its replicated intensity-independent changing-state effect and its unexpected overall intensity main effect against the set of seven prior experiments across four original articles, explicitly including Colle (1980; Journal of Verbal Learning and Verbal Behavior, 19(6), 722-735, DOI 10.1016/s0022-5371(80)90403-x). Shipped row 977 represents a different original paper (Tremblay & Jones, 1999, DOI 10.1037/0096-1523.25.4.1005), and sibling targets 1 and 2 are independent 1998 and 2008 studies by different authors in different journals; report equivalence does not apply. Addressing the prior adjudication and parent objection: all four original-target identities were accepted, while the prior source-scope hold concerned only per-original outcome disambiguation (because the Discussion notes that Colle's between-experiment intensity levels were not designed to evaluate overall intensity effects); outcome is not requested in this review and is set to cannot_be_determined.

corrected_value.title: Expecting to teach enhances motor learning and information processing during practice

decision.quote: The primary purpose of this research was to replicate the findings of Daou and colleagues (Daou, Lohse, et al., 2016; Daou, Buchanan, et al., 2016) Replications have been dichotomized into direct and conceptual categories (Makel et al., 2012) . According to Makel et al. (2012) direct replications seek to duplicate the original methods as closely as possible, whereas conceptual replications follow similar methods, but researchers purposefully modify features of the experimental protocol to test the rigor of the underlying hypotheses. Within this dichotomy, the approach adopted here aligned more with that of a direct replication. That is, we adopted the methods of the original experiment which first showed the effect (Daou, Buchanan, et al., 2016) , with the exception of including the more valid and reliable motivation and pressure measures that were used in their second experiment (Daou, Lohse, et al., 2016) .
decision.reason: No prior adjudication or state file exists for this work. The paper reports a preregistered replication (N = 76) explicitly retesting the golf-putting motor learning (retention radial error) and declarative free-recall advantages of expecting to teach reported across the first two experiments by Daou and colleagues: Daou, Buchanan, Lindsey, Lohse, & Miller (2016; Journal of Motor Learning and Development, 4(2), 197-207, DOI 10.1123/jmld.2015-0036) and Daou, Lohse, & Miller (2016; Human Movement Science, 49, 336-345, DOI 10.1016/j.humov.2016.08.009). In the Results and Discussion (including the TOST equivalence test against both original effect sizes, g = 1.08 and g = 0.82, and Table 6 comparing acquisition blocks across both studies), the authors directly evaluate and compare their data against both experiments. Shipped row 1065 covers only the first experiment (Daou, Buchanan, et al., 2016, DOI 10.1123/jmld.2015-0036); Daou, Lohse, & Miller (2016, DOI 10.1016/j.humov.2016.08.009) is a separate experiment with an independent sample, distinct acquisition and retention statistics, and additional IMI and motor preparation measures, so report equivalence does not apply.

decision.quote:
Data collection was replicated in 20 of
the original intervention sites in October 2005 to
assess whether programme delivery and impact continued an additional 12 months after initial training.
Results were positive, demonstrating that, with no
booster sessions, and despite both the loss of 13% of
trained teachers and differences among teachers in
the style of programme delivery, teachers continued
to deliver the programme into the third school year
after training and the gains made at 18 months in
pupil knowledge, self-efficacy and change in reported behaviours were replicated or improved on
with each new cohort of pupils [21].
The objective of this article is to assess whether
the gains made in pupil knowledge, self-efficacy
related to sexual restraint and condom use and behaviour change observed in 18- and 30-month
evaluations in Nyanza Province [18, 21] are replicated in diverse regions of the country.
decision.reason: As established in the prior adjudication, shipped row 61 (Maticka-Tyndale, Wildish, & Gichuru, 2007, Evaluation and Program Planning, 30(2), 172-186, DOI 10.1016/j.evalprogplan.2007.01.006, Reference 18, blind target_index 0) is the original 2002-2004 Nyanza Province randomized controlled trial evaluation of the Primary School Action for Better Health (PSABH) intervention across 40 matched pairs of schools. Candidate target_index 1 (Maticka-Tyndale, Wildish, & Gichuru, 2010, Sex Education, 10, 113-130, Reference 21) is not an independent original study, but a subsequent 30-month follow-up wave conducted in 20 of the exact same Nyanza intervention schools from Reference 18 to check whether the 18-month gains persisted an additional 12 months. The present paper (which collects baseline, 10-month, and 22-month data in five new regions) explicitly refers to Nyanza in the Abstract as 'the original impact evaluation conducted in Nyanza Province' and in the Limitations distinguishes 'the original [18]' from 'the subsequent results [21, 38]'. Because Reference 21 is a same-study follow-up wave of the Nyanza evaluation already represented by shipped row 61, no additional row is missing.

decision.quote: Overall findings of our first direct interview family study of obsessive–compulsive disorder (OCD) indicated that OCD is familial. In this replication study, we carefully examined the role of informant data in ascertaining OCD in relatives.
decision.reason: No prior adjudication or state file exists for this work. The replicating article (Lipsitz, Mannuzza, Chapman, Foa, Franklin, Goodwin, & Fyer, 2005, Psychological Medicine, DOI 10.1017/s003329170500543x) is titled 'A direct interview family study of obsessive–compulsive disorder. II. Contribution of proband informant information' and retests a single original study described in the abstract as 'our first direct interview family study of obsessive–compulsive disorder (OCD)'. That exact companion original study is already present in shipped row 886: Fyer, Lipsitz, Mannuzza, Aronowitz, & Chapman (2005), 'A direct interview family study of obsessive–compulsive disorder. I', Psychological Medicine, 35(11), 1611-1621, DOI 10.1017/s0033291705005441. Blind target_index 0 was left unmatched against shipped row 886 only because the supplied source text for 10.1017/s003329170500543x is abstract-only without a bibliography, causing the blind coder to leave the target citation fields empty.
